## Short version

A TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small per-core cache of recent virtual-to-physical address translations. On a big-memory server it covers under 1% of memory, so misses are frequent and each one is slow. Huge pages make each entry cover 2 MB or 1 GB instead of 4 KB, but they add memory-management risks.

## Words used here

- **Virtual address**: the address that a program uses.
- **Physical address**: the real location in RAM.
- **Page**: a fixed-size block of memory. The default size on x86-64 is 4 KB.
- **Page table**: a tree in RAM that maps virtual pages to physical pages. It has 4 levels, or 5 on recent server CPUs.
- **Page walk**: the CPU reads the page table level by level to find one translation.
- **TLB reach**: the number of TLB entries multiplied by the page size.
- **THP (Transparent Huge Pages)**: a Linux feature that creates 2 MB pages automatically.
- **hugetlb pool**: a fixed number of huge pages that the administrator reserves.
- **Compaction**: the kernel moves pages to build one contiguous free block.
- **NUMA node**: one CPU socket together with its local RAM.

## 1. What a TLB is

- A program uses virtual addresses. The CPU must translate each one to a physical address before it reads or writes.
- The translations are stored in the page table. The TLB keeps the most recent ones inside the core.
- A TLB hit adds almost no time. A TLB miss starts a page walk.

```
virtual      +-----+  hit
address ---> | TLB | ----------------------------> physical
             +-----+                               address
                | miss                               ^
                v                                    |
             +----+    +----+    +----+    +----+    |
             | L4 |--->| L3 |--->| L2 |--->| L1 |----+
             +----+    +----+    +----+    +----+
                         ^         ^         ^
                        1 GB      2 MB      4 KB
                        page      page      page
                      2 reads   3 reads   4 reads
```

The walk stops at the level that maps the page, so a larger page needs fewer reads. A fifth level adds one read to each walk.

## 2. Why misses are expensive on a big-memory server

The table uses an example server with 512 GB of RAM. The entry counts are typical for a recent Intel server core (est.).

| Page size | TLB entries (est.) | TLB reach | Share of 512 GB | Last-level table size for 512 GB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 KB | 2,048 | 8 MB | 0.0015% | 1 GB |
| 2 MB | 2,048 | 4 GB | 0.78% | 2 MB |
| 1 GB | 1,024 | 1,024 GB | 100% | 4 KB |

Insufficient data for your CPU: I did not read its TLB sizes. The `cpuid` command in section 5 prints them.

- The TLB size is fixed by the CPU design. It does not grow when you add RAM.
- With 4 KB pages, the last page-table level for 512 GB takes 1 GB. That does not fit in the CPU caches, so walk reads go to RAM.
- One read from RAM costs about 100 ns (est., about 300 CPU cycles).
- One miss needs up to 4 memory reads with 4 levels [Ref1]. The core caches the upper levels, so the last-level read usually dominates the cost.
- Inside a virtual machine, one miss can need up to 24 reads with 4 levels [Ref2].
- Big-memory workloads often access memory in random order. Examples are hash tables, database indexes, graphs and large lookup tables. Random order gives few TLB hits.
- On a multi-socket server, the page table can be on another NUMA node. Then each walk read takes longer.

A published study measured databases, in-memory caches and graph analytics. These workloads spent up to 10% of execution cycles on TLB misses, even with huge pages [Ref3].

## 3. How huge pages help

- One TLB entry covers 512 times more memory with 2 MB pages. With 1 GB pages it covers 262,144 times more.
- The page walk is shorter. A 2 MB page needs 3 reads and a 1 GB page needs 2 reads.
- The last page-table level for 512 GB shrinks from 1 GB to 2 MB. It then fits in the CPU caches, so the remaining walks are fast.
- The first access to new memory causes fewer page faults. One fault maps 2 MB instead of 4 KB, so the fault count is 512 times lower.
- In a virtual machine, both the guest and the host must use huge pages for the full gain.

Linux offers two ways to get huge pages:

| | THP | hugetlb pool |
|---|---|---|
| Who allocates | The kernel, automatically | The administrator, by reservation |
| Page sizes on x86-64 | 2 MB | 2 MB and 1 GB |
| Application change | None, or one `madvise` call | Explicit request, for example `mmap` with `MAP_HUGETLB` |
| Guarantee | None. It depends on contiguous free memory. | Guaranteed after the reservation succeeds |
| Can be swapped | Yes | No |

THP has three modes: `always`, `madvise` and `never` [Ref4]. In `madvise` mode, the application marks regions with the `madvise` system call. Only those regions get huge pages.

## 4. What can go wrong

### With THP

| What goes wrong | Why | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Long pauses | A page fault can wait while the kernel runs compaction to free a 2 MB block. | Set the THP `defrag` option to `defer` or `madvise` [Ref4]. |
| Memory use grows | An access to 1 byte allocates a full 2 MB page. khugepaged (the kernel thread that merges small pages) can also fill sparse regions [Ref8]. | Use `madvise` mode. Mark only regions that are fully used and long-lived. |
| Results vary between runs | THP needs contiguous free memory. That amount changes with uptime and with other users' load. | Record `AnonHugePages` with every performance run. |
| Freed memory returns late | An allocator frees 4 KB ranges inside a 2 MB page. The kernel can return that memory only after it splits the page. | Check the THP settings of your allocator. |
| Slower `fork` | After `fork` (the call that clones a process), a write can copy or split a 2 MB page. Redis documents latency problems from this [Ref7]. | Avoid `fork` in the huge-page process. |
| Slower first access | The kernel clears 2 MB per fault instead of 4 KB. | Access the memory once at startup. |

### With a hugetlb pool

| What goes wrong | Why | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Other work loses memory | Reserved pages cannot serve normal allocations, even when they are idle [Ref5]. | Size the pool from measured need. On a shared server, agree the size with the other users. |
| Reservation is partial | A reservation at run time needs contiguous free memory. The kernel reserves fewer pages without an error. | Reserve at boot, mainly for 1 GB pages. Then read `HugePages_Total`. |
| Process fails at startup or later | With too few free pages, `mmap` (the memory-mapping system call) fails. Without a reservation, the first access raises SIGBUS (a signal that normally kills the process) [Ref6]. | Access all huge-page memory at startup. |
| Pages on the wrong NUMA node | The kernel spreads the pool across nodes. A process bound to one node can use up that node's share. | Set the page count per node under `/sys/devices/system/node/` [Ref5]. |
| Application must change | The application must request pool pages explicitly. | Plan the code change and a fallback path to 4 KB pages. |

### With both

- A workload with small or sequential memory use already has few TLB misses. Huge pages gain little there.
- Some CPUs have few TLB entries for 1 GB pages. Then 1 GB pages can gain less than 2 MB pages.

Recommended starting point: THP in `madvise` mode on the large regions. Move to a hugetlb pool only when you need guaranteed coverage or 1 GB pages.

## 5. Checks to propose in the review

```bash
# TLB sizes of this CPU
cpuid -1 | grep -i tlb

# Share of cycles with a page walk in progress (Intel event names)
perf stat -e cycles,dtlb_load_misses.walk_active,dtlb_store_misses.walk_active \
    -p <pid> -- sleep 30

# Huge-page mode and use
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
grep -i huge /proc/meminfo
grep -E 'thp_fault_alloc|thp_fault_fallback|compact_stall' /proc/vmstat
```

1. Before the change, divide `walk_active` by `cycles`. That share is about the upper limit of the TLB gain.
2. After the change, confirm that huge pages are in use. `AnonHugePages` shows THP use and `HugePages_Free` shows pool use.
3. Compare `thp_fault_fallback` and `compact_stall` before and after. Rising counts mean failed huge-page requests or pauses from compaction.

Insufficient data on your workload: I have no measurement of its page-walk share. Step 1 gives it.

## References

- [Ref1] Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Volume 3A, chapter "Paging".
- [Ref2] Bhargava, Serebrin, Spadini, Manne. "Accelerating Two-Dimensional Page Walks for Virtualized Systems." ASPLOS 2008.
- [Ref3] Basu, Gandhi, Chang, Hill, Swift. "Efficient Virtual Memory for Big Memory Servers." ISCA 2013.
- [Ref4] Linux kernel documentation, "Transparent Hugepage Support". https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html
- [Ref5] Linux kernel documentation, "HugeTLB Pages". https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/hugetlbpage.html
- [Ref6] Linux kernel documentation, "Hugetlbfs Reservation". https://docs.kernel.org/mm/hugetlbfs_reserv.html
- [Ref7] Redis documentation, "Diagnosing latency issues", section on transparent huge pages. https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/latency/
- [Ref8] Kwon, Yu, Peter, Rossbach, Witchel. "Coordinated and Efficient Huge Page Management with Ingens." OSDI 2016.
